items.prompt: He refreshed the inbox again, then again, then closed the laptop and opened it immediately, as if the answer he needed might arrive in the half-second the screen was dark.
She clapped the loudest when her sister crossed the stage, gripping her program so tightly the edges curled, smiling at everyone who looked her way.
Every September he drove the long way home just to pass the school, slowing near the oak where the crossing guard used to stand.
She laughed at his jokes the same as always, passed the salt without being asked, and never once mentioned she had read the message.
He set two placemats out of habit, caught himself, folded one back into the drawer, then ate standing at the counter instead.
She let them finish telling the story about the summit before mentioning, quietly, that she had reached it first, two years ago, in February.
He bought the same brand of orange juice she had preferred and let it expire at the back of the fridge, untouched, three times running.
She returned the twenty dollars before he noticed it was missing, tucking it into his jacket pocket and saying nothing for the rest of the week.
He checked the flight status before bed, then once more at midnight, then left his shoes by the door so he would not have to look for them in the morning.
She answered his calls now, short and polite at first, then longer, until one afternoon she found herself laughing at something he said and did not apologize for it.
She took every extra shift, enrolled in the night class, and introduced herself at the party using the title she did not yet hold.
He kept the receipt for the jacket he never bought her folded inside his wallet, soft at the creases now, unspendable.
He refreshed the inbox again, then again, then closed the laptop and opened it thirty seconds later, hands not quite steady.
She laughed a little too loudly at his joke, then spent the drive home listing every word she had said wrong.
Every night he set two glasses on the table before remembering, then stood there a moment before putting one back.
She watched her sister open the promotion letter, smiled wide, and went to the bathroom to sit on the cold floor for a while.
He still knew the bus route by heart, could name every stop, though the city had rerouted it nine years ago.
She answered every question he asked her, clearly, completely, and never once looked at his face while she spoke.
He ate dinner at the counter, television on full volume, and still heard the particular silence of the second bedroom.
She pressed her daughter's medal flat against her palm on the train home, not showing anyone, just holding it.
He called his mother after the diagnosis was cleared and talked about the weather for twenty minutes, voice bright and unsteady.
She used to call him when she needed someone; now she scrolled to his name, watched it sit there, and put the phone face-down.
He signed up for the six a.m. shift, took the unpaid course on weekends, and introduced himself to everyone senior to him in the room.
She kept the acceptance letter in a drawer she never opened, beneath things she no longer needed but could not throw away.
He refreshed the inbox every few minutes, not because he expected anything, but because the small act kept the possibility alive.
She laughed loudest at his jokes when the new colleague was watching, and touched his arm a half-second too long.
He drove the long way home just to pass the house with the yellow door, the one that had belonged to his grandmother.
She told the story at dinner as though it had happened to a friend, watching her mother's face for the exact moment recognition landed.
He set the alarm fifteen minutes early every day for a year and then quietly stopped setting it at all.
She read the apology twice, folded it, and put it in the drawer with his letters instead of the bin.
He stood at the edge of every group photo, hands in pockets, already half-turned toward the door before the shutter clicked.
She checked the lock three times, then stood in the dark hallway listening to a silence she couldn't quite trust.
He wore the tie to the school run, even though no one there knew he had been promoted.
She kept the ticket stub from a city she never went back to in the pocket of a coat she still wore.
He told the new version so many times he had almost stopped remembering the afternoon he agreed and then said nothing.
She exhaled slowly in the car park, hands still gripping the wheel, before going back inside to be normal again.
She refreshed the page again, counted the names below hers, and opened a new tab to check whether the committee chair had posted anything recently.
He laughed at the joke a half-second after everyone else, watching their faces first to make sure it was the right kind of laugh.
Every few blocks she slowed down without meaning to, glancing at doorways she had no reason to enter, reading menus of restaurants she would never visit.
He kept the receipt in his wallet for six weeks, folded so small the numbers were nearly invisible, moving it from one card slot to another each time he switched wallets.
She stood a little straighter when her daughter's name appeared on the screen, and had to press her lips together before she could say anything at all.
He booked the flights, then cancelled them, then looked up the departure times again at two in the morning just to feel the possibility sitting there.
She sat very still while her sister described the holiday, nodding at the photographs, asking one careful question about a restaurant she already knew she would never go to.
He answered her call on the first ring, said it was fine, said really it was fine, and after they hung up sat with the phone face-down on the table for a long time.
She pulled the old playlist up, didn't press play, just scrolled the song titles slowly with her thumb the way you'd run a hand along a fence you used to climb.
He drove the long way home every evening that week, arriving just after the meeting would have ended, always surprised to find the lights already off.
She put his letters in a box, moved the box to the garage, then brought it inside again and put it on the same shelf but behind the encyclopedias.
He ordered the thing he had almost ordered for thirty years, ate it slowly, and did not look up when the waiter asked if everything was all right.
He checked the door lock three times, then checked it again from the car, then sat in the parking lot for six minutes before finally driving away.
She laughed a little too loudly at his joke, then went quiet watching his hand rest near the other woman's wrist.
